```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(fpp3)
library(BVAR)
```

### 2.1 a.
```{r}
liquor_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/MRTSSM4453USN.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    MRTSSM4453USN = col_double()
  )
)

liquor <- liquor_raw |>
  transmute(Month = yearmonth(observation_date), sales = MRTSSM4453USN) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month) |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2019 Dec"))

has_gaps(liquor)
```

### 2.1 b.
```{r}
p_sales <- liquor |> autoplot(sales) + labs(
    title = "U.S. Beer, Wine, and Liquor Retail Sales",
    subtitle = "Not seasonally adjusted, millions of dollars",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Sales ($ Millions)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
print(p_sales)

p_season <- liquor |>
  gg_season(log(sales)) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Plot of Log Retail Sales",
    subtitle = "Beer, Wine, and Liquor Stores",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Log(Sales)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
print(p_season)
```
The graphs shows the lowest point of sales to be around January, with a steady upward trend through most of the year, with the highest point of sales coming in December. The magnitude of the frequencies also grow, which could mean that creating a similar Retail Sales graph with log values could be helpful.

### 2.2 a.
```{r}
liquor_fit <- liquor |>
  model(arima = ARIMA(log(sales)),
        ets   = ETS(log(sales)))

liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> report()
liquor_fit |> select(ets) |> report()
```

```{r}
### 2.2 b.
liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> gg_tsresiduals()

liquor_fit |>
  select(arima) |>
  augment() |> 
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24, dof = 4)
```

### 2.3 a.
```{r}
liquor_cv <- liquor |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 120, .step = 1) |>
  filter(.id < max(.id))

liquor_cv_fit <- liquor_cv |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(sales),
        ets    = ETS(log(sales)),
        arima  = ARIMA(log(sales)))

#saveRDS(liquor_cv_fit, "results/liquor_cv_fit.rds")
liquor_cv_fit <- readRDS("results/liquor_cv_fit.rds")
saveRDS(liquor_cv_fit, file = "results/liquor_cv_fit.rds")
```

With 336 total months in the sample, a 120-month initial training window, the cross-validation will evaluate 216 forecast origins.
  
### 2.3 b.
```{r}
liquor_cv_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |> knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

The first forecast is for January 2002, and the last forecast is for December 2019. Both RMSE and MAE support that ARIMA and ETS outperform the seasonal naive benchmark.

### 2.4
```{r}
liquor_errs <- liquor_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(liquor) |> select(Month, actual = sales),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e)

forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets, h = 1, power = 2)
```
### Arima v ETS
```{r}
dm_arima_ets <- forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets, h = 1, power = 2)
dm_arima_ets
```
### Arima v Snaive
```{r}
dm_arima_snaive <- forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$snaive, h = 1, power = 2)
dm_arima_snaive
```

The Diebold-Mariano test comparing ARIMA and ETS yields a DM statistic of -2.91 with a p-value of 0.0040 indicates that ARIMA's accuracy is significantly better than ETS. We also see that the ARIMA model performs much better than the seasonal naive model which has a DM-stat of -10.755, worst of all the comparisons. 

## Part 3 

### 3 a. 
```{r}
liquor_combo_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  mutate(combo = (arima + ets) / 2) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_combo_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE))

liquor_combo_fc |> knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

The equal-weight combo yields an RMSE and MAE that tracks or slightly improves upon the best individual model, acting as a block against model specification error.

### 3 b. 
```{r}
err_corr <- cor(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets)
err_corr
```

The forecast errors between ARIMA and ETS are very strongly correlated  because both models capture the exact same trend and seasonal patterns. Because similar models make correlated errors, averaging them won't reduce errors making the individual model better.

## Part 4

### 4.1 a.
```{r}
qd_raw <- read_csv("data/fredqd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  slice(-(1:2))
```

### 4.1 b.
```{r}
growth <- function(x) 100 * difference(log(x))
qd <- qd_raw |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y")) |>
  transmute(date,
            gdp    = growth(GDPC1),     # real GDP
            cons   = growth(PCECC96),   # real consumption
            inv    = growth(GPDIC1),    # real investment
            emp    = growth(PAYEMS),    # payroll employment
            infl   = growth(GDPCTPI),   # GDP price index
            unrate = difference(UNRATE),     # unemployment rate
            ffr    = difference(FEDFUNDS),   # federal funds rate
            gs10   = difference(GS10)) |>    # 10-year Treasury yield
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

y <- qd |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()

nrow(y)
head(y)
```

### 4.1 c.
```{r}
N <- nrow(y)
origins <- 120:(N - 1)
actual <- y[121:N, ]
```
With 240 quarterly observations 1960 Q1 - 2019 Q4 and origins running from 120 to 239, we produce 120 forecasts for each variable. The first forecast is for March 1, 1990 or 1990 Q1 and the last forecast is for 2019 Q4 which is December 1, 2019.
  
### 4.2
```{r}
var_ols_fc <- function(z, p) {
  e <- embed(z, p + 1)            # columns: y_t, then its lags 1 to p
  M <- ncol(z)                    # number of variables
  B <- coef(lm(e[, 1:M] ~ e[, -(1:M)]))
  x <- c(1, t(z[nrow(z):(nrow(z) - p + 1), ]))   # constant, latest p lags
  x %*% B
}

fc_var1 <- NULL
fc_var4 <- NULL
for (T in origins) {
  fc_var1 <- rbind(fc_var1, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 1))
  fc_var4 <- rbind(fc_var4, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 4))
}

rmse_by_var <- function(f) sqrt(colMeans((actual - f)^2))
rmse_by_var(fc_var1)
rmse_by_var(fc_var4)
```
The VAR(1) forecasts better for 7 out of the 8 variables, only inflation (infl) slightly favoring VAR(4). Even though VAR(4) nests VAR(1), estimating 264 parameters with OLS creates a lot of out-of-sample estimation variance, while the smaller VAR(1) avoids overfitting with a smaller sample.

## 4.3 a.
```{r}
bvar_cv <- function(lambda) {
  pr <- bv_priors(hyper = "lambda",
                  mn = bv_mn(lambda = bv_lambda(mode = lambda, sd = 0.4,
                                                min = 0.999 * lambda,
                                                max = 1.001 * lambda),
                             b = 0))
  fc <- NULL
  for (T in origins) {
    fit_T <- bvar(y[1:T, ], lags = 4, priors = pr,
                  n_draw = 2000, n_burn = 1000, verbose = FALSE)
    x <- c(1, t(y[T:(T - 3), ]))         # constant and 4 lags of each variable
    fc <- rbind(fc, x %*% coef(fit_T))   # forecast of y_{T+1}
  }
  fc
}

set.seed(422)
fc_bvar_03 <- bvar_cv(0.3)
saveRDS(fc_bvar_03, "results/fc_bvar_03.rds")
```

## 4.3 b.
```{r}
set.seed(422)
fc_bvar_005 <- bvar_cv(0.05)
saveRDS(fc_bvar_005, "results/fc_bvar_005.rds")

var_results <- tibble(
  Variable = colnames(y),
  `VAR(1)` = rmse_by_var(fc_var1),
  `VAR(4)` = rmse_by_var(fc_var4),
  `BVAR(4), lambda = 0.3` = rmse_by_var(fc_bvar_03),
  `BVAR(4), lambda = 0.05` = rmse_by_var(fc_bvar_005)
)

saveRDS(var_results, "results/var_results.rds")

var_results <- readRDS("results/var_results.rds")
var_results |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```
Compared to the OLS VAR(4), the BVAR(4) with lambda = 0.3 shrinks unstable higher-lag coefficients toward zero because of the Minnesota prior, lowering out-of-sample RMSE and performing competitively with the VAR(1). When lambda = 0.05 and the shrinking is compresses coefficients even harder, which can drive errors back up if too extreme. Finally, the best RMSE in the table is not a fair estimate because picking the best hyperparameter lambda based on test-set performance creates selection bias.

### 4.3 c.
```{r}
e_var4 <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_var4[, 1]
e_bvar <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_bvar_03[, 1]
forecast::dm.test(e_var4, e_bvar, h = 1, power = 2)

col_idx <- which(colnames(y) == "infl")
e_var4_infl <- actual[, col_idx] - fc_var4[, col_idx]
e_bvar_infl <- actual[, col_idx] - fc_bvar_03[, col_idx]
forecast::dm.test(e_var4_infl, e_bvar_infl, h = 1, power = 2)
```
The DM tests comparing the VAR(4) to the BVAR(4) for GDP growth and inflation evaluate whether the differences in squared-error loss are significant at a 1-quarter horizon.

## Part 5

### 5.1 a.
```{r}
md_raw <- read_csv("data/fredmd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
tcode <- unlist(md_raw[1, -1])
md <- md_raw[-1, ] |> mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y"))

transform_series <- function(x, code) {
  d <- function(v) c(NA, diff(v))
  switch(as.character(code),
         "1" = x,                      # level
         "2" = d(x),                   # first difference
         "3" = d(d(x)),                # second difference
         "4" = log(x),                 # log
         "5" = 100 * d(log(x)),        # growth rate
         "6" = 100 * d(d(log(x))),     # change in the growth rate
         "7" = d(x / dplyr::lag(x) - 1))
}
```

### 5.1 b.
```{r}
fm <- map2_dfc(md[names(tcode)], tcode, transform_series) |>
  mutate(date = md$date, .before = 1) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

fm <- fm[, colSums(is.na(fm)) == 0]

dim(fm)
```

### 5.1 c.
```{r}
tcode[c("INDPRO", "PAYEMS", "CPIAUCSL", "FEDFUNDS")]
```

INDPRO and PAYEMS use code 5 (monthly percentage growth rate, 100 * Delta * log(x)) to remove upward trends. CPIAUCSL uses code 6 (the change in monthly inflation, 100 * Delta^2 * log(x)) because price levels require differencing to become stationary. FEDFUNDS uses code 2 (simple first difference, Delta * x) rather than logs because interest rates are already measured in percentage units rather than growing unit levels.

### 5.2 a.
```{r}
Z <- fm |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()

pc <- prcomp(scale(Z))

summary(pc)$importance[, 1:5]
```

The three principal components explain 29.5% of the total variation across all 121 series: PC1 = 15.0%, PC2 = 7.4%, PC3 = 7.1%.

### 5.2 b.
```{r}
F1 <- pc$x[, 1] * sign(cor(pc$x[, 1], fm$INDPRO))

tibble(date = fm$date, F1 = F1) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, F1)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "First Factor from FRED-MD", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### 5.2 c.
```{r}
sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 1], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 2], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
```

Based on the highest absolute correlations, Factor 1 captures broad economic activity and business cycle fluctuations, and its top series consist entirely of payroll employment and industrial production. Factor 2 captures aggregate price changes and inflation, its top series are mostly consumer price indices and PCE price deflators. 

### 5.3
```{r}
ip <- fm$INDPRO
n <- nrow(Z)
init <- which(fm$date == as.Date("1989-12-01"))

e_ar <- NULL
e_fa <- NULL
for (T in init:(n - 1)) {
  F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:3]         # factors using data through T
  d <- data.frame(y_next = ip[2:T], y = ip[1:(T - 1)], F_T[1:(T - 1), ])
  new <- data.frame(y = ip[T], t(F_T[T, ]))
  e_ar <- c(e_ar, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ y, d), new))
  e_fa <- c(e_fa, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ ., d), new))
}

c(RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)))
```
The horse race yields an RMSE of 0.617 for the AR(1) and 0.589 for the factor-augmented model, confirming the class result. Estimating factors once on the full 1960–2019 sample would create data leakage and allow for information that should be unavailable at the time.

### 5.4
```{r}
direct_race <- function(series, h = 12, r = 3) {
  lv <- md |>
    mutate(log_x = log(.data[[series]]),
           g = 100 * (log_x - lag(log_x))) |>
    filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))
  yh <- 100 * (lead(lv$log_x, h) - lv$log_x)      # growth over the next h months
  g  <- lv$g                                      # growth over the latest month
  
  e_ar <- NULL
  e_fa <- NULL
  for (T in init:(n - h)) {
    F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:r, drop = FALSE]
    i <- 1:(T - h)
    d <- data.frame(yh = yh[i], g = g[i], F_T[i, , drop = FALSE])
    new <- data.frame(g = g[T], F_T[T, , drop = FALSE])
    e_ar <- c(e_ar, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ g, d), new))
    e_fa <- c(e_fa, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ ., d), new))
  }
  tibble(series, forecasts = length(e_ar),
         RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)),
         MAE_AR = mean(abs(e_ar)), MAE_FA = mean(abs(e_fa)),
         DM_pvalue = forecast::dm.test(e_ar, e_fa, h = h, power = 2,
                                       varestimator = "bartlett")$p.value)
}

direct_race("CPIAUCSL")
```
Yes, adding the factors improves the 12-month CPI inflation forecast, reducing the RMSE from 2.108 to 1.894 which is significant becuase of a p-value less than 0.001.
